newsitem.title: USA: Big World Bank loan to help 15 million Russians.
newsitem.headline: Big World Bank loan to help 15 million Russians.

text.p: An $800 million World Bank loan, the third biggest in the history of the organisation, should accelerate Russian reforms and improve living standards for 15 million people, World Bank officials said on Thursday.

Regional vice president Johannes Linn told a news conference that the loan would help fund much-needed changes to Russia's unwieldy system of payments for pensions, unemployment benefits and child benefits.
"It is the largest World Bank loan to a country in my region -- eastern Europe and central Asia -- and it is the third largest loan in the bank's history," he said.

"This is a very important pillar of a package to accelerate structural reform which the Russian authorities are undertaking ... This programme will improve living standards for about 15 million Russians."
Wage and pension arrears worth billions of dollars have been one of Russia's most pressing economic problems, and repeated efforts to resolve the crisis have come to nothing.

But reform chief Anatoly Chubais said on Thursday that money to repay budget debts to pensioners had been transferred in full. "By July 1 not a single ruble will be owed to a single pensioner," he told a Cabinet meeting.

Previous government arguments that newly privatised companies are to blame for many of the wage and pension arrears have failed to convince millions of people that it is worth pressing on with painful economic reforms.
Officials admit that over 20 percent of Russians are living below the poverty line.
Linn described social reforms as the next critical step of the overall reform programme, designed to create a free-market economy modelled on that in the West.
"Arrears to the population are to be paid off under the programme and steps will be taken to ensure that they do not occur again," he said.

Linn said the first $300 million instalment of the new loan would be paid immediately, but two further $250 million tranches would only be released if the Russian authorities met a string of conditions.

One condition of paying the second instalment was that the government draw up a policy document on options for pension reform, while release of the final tranche would depend on new pension laws being submitted to parliament.
Russia's reformist government already finds it hard to get legislation through the State Duma lower house of parliament, which is dominated by communists and other conservatives.
"If we would have made this loan conditional on approval from parliament, it would have been a four- or five-year loan," said Linn.
He said the submission of the pension plan to parliament had originally been scheduled for December, but it was not now expected until the spring of 1998.
The World Bank, which earlier this month approved six loans to Russia worth a total of almost $900 million, has said it could lend Russia $6 billion over the next two years.
